issues.description: Method name/signature mismatch for the 3-qubit QFT implementation. The problem tasks and the solution implementation use a method named qft_circuit (and qft_circuit_inverse for the inverse), but the template defines the forward transform as _qft_circuit (leading underscore) while providing qft_circuit_inverse. This difference in the forward-method name is structural (not just a missing body) and will confuse students and break automated tests or example usage that expects qft_circuit to exist. The solution's qft_circuit_inverse calls qft_circuit, which the template does not expose, preventing a straightforward student implementation and making the template incompatible with the solution reference.
issues.suggested_fix: Rename the template method _qft_circuit to qft_circuit (remove the leading underscore) so its name/signature matches the solution and the expected API. Ensure qft_circuit_inverse in the template calls qft_circuit (or otherwise matches the solution) so students and tests have a consistent forward and inverse QFT API.

issues.description: The 3-qubit QFT method name is inconsistent between artifacts: the template defines the forward QFT method as _qft_circuit (leading underscore) while the solution implements it as qft_circuit. The problem statement tasks refer to implementing the QFT (Exercise 6.1 / test_ex1_qft_circuit) without an underscore, which aligns with the solution name. This mismatch can confuse students about which method to implement or reuse (and may break expected reuse from qft_circuit_inverse), creating unnecessary mapping friction between the exercise description, the starter code, and the reference solution.
issues.suggested_fix: Align the forward QFT method name across artifacts. Best fix: rename the template method from _qft_circuit to qft_circuit so the template, problem task name (Exercise 6.1), and solution all use the same identifier. Alternatively, update qft_circuit_inverse in the template to call _qft_circuit (and document the underscore convention), but the first option is clearer for students and avoids accidental 'private' naming confusion.
